name: Southern US English
summary: Southern US English is a family of accents spoken across the American South. Its most audible features are vowel changes: a monophthongised PRICE vowel (the 'I' sound in 'ride' or 'my' is said as one open vowel), a weakened glide, fronted back vowels, and a 'drawl' in which stressed short vowels are stretched into two parts. Grammar differences are few and mostly limited to y'all, double modals (might could) and fixin' to. Most of the difference is in sound, so spelling changes should stay minimal. Several features are documented as declining, especially among younger and urban speakers. Evidence here comes from Wikipedia summaries (checked against the Yale Grammatical Diversity Project for modals). Primary academic sources (Labov, Ash and Boberg, Atlas of North American English; the Dictionary of American Regional English) were not opened in this pass and should be checked before the file is treated as final.

grammar.condition: Only when addressing two or more people. Do not use for one person.
grammar.example_standard: Are you coming to dinner tonight?
grammar.example_dialect: Are y'all coming to dinner tonight?

grammar.condition: Addressing several groups that are separate from each other. Rare; use at most once in a monologue, and only if the scene calls for it.

grammar.standard: might be able to / could possibly
grammar.condition: Double modal (two modal verbs in a row). Most common in South Midland and Southern speech. The Yale project reports it is generally not stigmatized but usage frequency varies a lot between speakers.
grammar.example_standard: I might be able to help you.

grammar.standard: be about to / be going to (near future)
grammar.condition: Near future for an action that is about to happen. Informal.

pronunciation.rule: PRICE vowel is monophthongised: the 'I' vowel (as in 'ride', 'my', 'time') loses its glide and is said as one open vowel, in many or all environments.
pronunciation.actor_tip: Start with an open 'ah' and hold it steady. Do not slide up toward 'ee'. Say 'my' as one clean open sound. This is the single most recognizable Southern vowel, so use it on every 'I' and 'my' but do not overdo it.

pronunciation.rule: Pin-pen merger: before the nasal consonants m, n and ng, the vowels of 'pin' and 'pen' are the same, so the two words sound identical.
pronunciation.actor_tip: In words with m, n or ng after the vowel, use one shared vowel (a relaxed 'ih' that is close to 'eh'). 'Let's go to the pen' should sound like 'pin'. Do not apply this before other consonants: 'bet' and 'bit' stay different.
pronunciation.example: pin / pen, kin / ken, him / hem, tin / ten

pronunciation.rule: Mary-merry merger (partial): 'Mary' and 'merry' share the same vowel, while 'marry' may keep its own vowel. Most common in the South, especially Louisiana.
pronunciation.ipa: /ˈmɛri/ for both Mary and merry; marry may keep /ˈmæri/ (approximate)
pronunciation.actor_tip: Say 'Mary' and 'merry' with the same vowel, as in 'merry'. Keep 'marry' with the short 'a' of 'cat'. Use only if the monologue contains these words; it is a subtle feature, so do not force it.

pronunciation.rule: Back vowels are fronted: the vowels in GOAT, GOOSE, STRUT and FOOT are pronounced further forward in the mouth than in General American.
pronunciation.ipa: No exact IPA in source. Fronting of /oʊ/, /uː/, /ʌ/, /ʊ/ (direction only)
pronunciation.actor_tip: Keep the same vowel but move the tongue forward in the mouth. 'Go', 'you', 'cup' and 'good' should sit toward the front. Do not make them sound like different words.

pronunciation.rule: Drawl: stressed short vowels, especially in emphasised words, get an extra glide and become two-part vowels.
pronunciation.ipa: Approximate, from source examples: /ɛ/ -> [eɪ] ('pet' as 'pay-et'); /ɪ/ -> [iɪ] ('pit' as 'pee-it')
pronunciation.actor_tip: Stretch only the one word you want to emphasise, not every word in the line. Say 'pet' as 'pay-et' and 'pit' as 'pee-it'. A drawl on every word becomes a caricature.

pronunciation.rule: Historic r-dropping: traditional older rural speakers, and many Black Southern speakers, drop /r/ after vowels or before consonants. Current white Southern speech has become more rhotic (pronounced r) overall.
pronunciation.actor_tip: For an older rural character, let the r in 'car', 'door' and 'floor' fade so it sounds like 'cah' and 'doe'. For a younger or urban character, keep the r. Decide per character, not per monologue.

common_mistakes: Stretching every vowel in the line (the 'Foghorn' caricature). The drawl is for stressed words only.
Using y'all to address one person.
Dropping every r in every word regardless of character age or region (r-dropping is documented as declining).
Piling on ain't, fixin' to, y'all and bless your heart in one speech. Choose one or two.
Spelling every word in dialect (e.g. 'gonna', 'yer'). The accent is in the sound, not the spelling. Use the sound rules instead.
Sugary 'Southern belle' delivery applied to every character. Tone and class vary widely across the South.
generational_notes: Source describes the Southern accent as in gradual decline, especially among younger and urban speakers; rural white speakers keep more features.
Historic r-dropping is the clearest example of decline. Current white Southern speakers have become more rhotic.
PRICE monophthongisation and glide weakening are documented as the most defining features of the current Southern accent, but the source does not give age-by-age frequency figures.
Double modals, y'all and fixin' to are presented in the source as widely used and not heavily stigmatized, with large variation between speakers.
conversion_guidelines: Decide first whether the character is older/rural, middle-aged, or young/urban. Apply historic r-dropping only to older/rural characters, and keep r for young/urban characters.
Apply the PRICE rule (my, ride, time, I) consistently, but do not use it on every word that contains an 'I' sound in one line.
Apply the pin-pen merger only before m, n and ng. Never before other consonants.
Apply the drawl to one stressed word per line at most.
Use no more than two grammar markers in a monologue. Prefer one of: y'all (group address), fixin' to (near future), might could (hedged ability).
Keep spelling close to standard English. Do not apostrophise words just to signal an accent, except for the grammar items above.
Vocabulary: use at most two or three Southern words per monologue, chosen where they fit the character.
In stage notes, list which rules were applied so the actor can practise each one separately.
